answer.exemplar: The factor gamma, which is one over the square root of one minus the square of the speed ratio, multiplies both the energy and the momentum of a massive particle. It is finite at any speed below that of light but tends without bound as the speed approaches it, and it is exactly infinite at that speed. The total energy of a particle is gamma m c squared, so the energy needed to reach a given speed is finite for every subluminal speed and infinite at light speed itself. There is no finite amount of energy that does the job, and the series expansion makes the same point: for speeds much smaller than that of light the kinetic energy is very nearly half m v squared, but at a ratio of ${gam} the energy is dominated by the gamma factor and the speed is ${vAt} m per s, hardly different from its starting value. The energy that keeps being supplied is therefore not converted into speed but into momentum, since the momentum grows as gamma times m times v while the speed changes by ever smaller amounts. This is why particle accelerators need ever larger rings to reach higher energies, why no rocket can reach that speed, and why the whole scheme of ordinary mechanics fails completely at the boundary. The limit is not a rule imposed on the theory from outside; it falls out of the requirement that the speed of light be the same in every frame, which forces the factor gamma into the equations, and the factor diverges exactly where the frame transformation would cease to make sense.

questions.explanation: A good answer starts from the two postulates, since the limit is a consequence of them rather than an extra assumption. The first says the laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame, and the second says the speed of light is the same in all of them. Applying the classical rule for adding velocities to a light ray would make its speed different in a moving frame, so the classical rule has to be replaced, and the replacement introduces the factor gamma. That factor multiplies the energy and the momentum of anything with a rest mass, it is finite below the speed of light, and it diverges exactly at it, so the energy required to reach light speed is infinite. A strong answer then explains where the energy goes, which is into momentum rather than into speed, because for speeds close to that of light a fixed extra energy produces an ever smaller change in speed. A convincing answer should also link the divergence to the cost in practice, in the growing size of accelerators, and should make clear that no amount of energy changes the conclusion. Answers that simply assert a speed limit, or that claim light has a special push, miss the mechanism entirely.
